jtbd.functional: Get a meal with the least effort, time, and cost.
jtbd.emotional: Satisfy a craving or treat myself.
jtbd.social: Order for — or with — other people.

pains.t: Forcing location before value is a friction point for new food delivery users.
pains.w: Onboarding demands a location before showing anything useful. Evidence is split — some users accept it as normal for a food app, others resent being blocked from exploring — but for explore-first newcomers it's a barrier.

pains.t: The sign-up wall, not the location step, is the real blocker to exploration.
pains.w: New food delivery users want to browse before committing, but the app forces sign-up/sign-in early and the Skip/X option lacks context, so they feel trapped into registering.

pains.t: A cluttered first screen overwhelms new food delivery users.
pains.w: For first-time visitors the homescreen is busy and hard to parse, adding cognitive load at the most important moment — the first impression.

pains.t: Language and translation gaps drive expat food delivery users to churn.
pains.w: Inconsistent translations (especially in menus and swimlanes) leave expats confused about shops vs. groceries, and can push them to churn before they even install.

pains.t: The app isn't perceived as accessible, shutting out A11Y food delivery users early.
pains.w: Accessibility users find the app hard to navigate and the menu overwhelming with assistive tech, disempowering them during discovery.

pains.t: Cost is the #1 reason food delivery users don't order at all.
pains.w: Money concerns are the single most common barrier (44%): ordering is seen as pricier than cooking or eating out, so price-sensitive users opt out before they browse.

pains.t: Deal discovery is the hardest task in the whole journey for food delivery users.
pains.w: Incentives have no single entry point and low visibility — in SEQ testing, finding a promotion scores as the hardest job of all — so users scroll and hunt for deals.

pains.t: Incentive clutter makes offers read as noise, not help.
pains.w: A crowded, uncoordinated wall of banners forces food delivery users to scan them one by one, so deals feel like clutter rather than value.

quote.text: It looks complicated. There's no united UI, the banners are separated, so I have to look one by one.

pains.t: Pro's value is unclear, so food delivery users don't subscribe even when it pays off.
pains.w: ~1 in 5 users never subscribe despite ordering enough to break even, and ~53% of subscribers churn on low perceived value; benefits feel murky and Pro prompts even reach ineligible users.

pains.t: Loyalty feels weaker than competitors' to food delivery users.
pains.w: Rivals' loyalty schemes — points, cross-service perks, clear home-screen value — are perceived as stronger and easier to grasp than Pandora's.

delights.t: An easy sign-up gets new food delivery users to a first order fast.
delights.w: Registration is called straightforward, helping newcomers reach a first order without friction.

delights.t: Popular restaurants give new and indecisive food delivery users an easy way in.
delights.w: Popular-restaurant and social-proof recommendations lower the effort of starting, matching what less-decisive users rely on to choose.

jtbd.functional: Find something I'll enjoy fast — matching my craving, my budget, and worth the money — without opening every restaurant.
jtbd.emotional: Decide with confidence and avoid the frustration of a disappointing order.
jtbd.social: Use other people's ratings and reviews to trust a place I haven't tried.

pains.t: Search returns the wrong results for food delivery users.
pains.w: A cuisine or dish search surfaces vendors that don't match (drinks for 'pizza', mostly non-Indian for 'Indian'), eroding trust in the assortment and driving drop-off.

quote.text: I searched for Indian and here is everything but indian. 4-5 restaurants before 2 indian options come up.

pains.t: Vendors without the searched dish still appear in results.
pains.w: Restaurants that don't carry the dish show up with no explanation, so food delivery users click through only to find it isn't there.

quote.text: It's not helpful when you typed in vegetarian (pizza) and the first thing you see is meat (pizza).

pains.t: The app is restaurant-first, but food delivery users think dish-first.
pains.w: Two-thirds open with a dish or cuisine in mind, yet discovery routes them through restaurants — extra steps against a dish-led goal.

quote.text: It would be more logical to display the restaurants and the specific dish that's available in the restaurant.

pains.t: Filters are hard to find and go unused — under 5% of sessions.
pains.w: Most food delivery users don't notice filters, and long cuisine lists plus distrusted dietary filters make narrowing tiring when they do.

quote.text: This is a lot of scrolling. Tell your colleagues I don't like scrolling too much.

pains.t: Cross-vendor comparison is a critical, unmet need for food delivery users.
pains.w: Comparing the same dish across vendors on price, quality and deals means backing out and re-entering each store — web users even open a browser tab per restaurant to do it.

quote.text: I couldn't do comparison across shops, and it would be helpful to compare products across shops for prices, packaging, details.

pains.t: The real price stays hidden until food delivery users open a menu.
pains.w: The $ signal doesn't show actual prices or minimum order value, so users open a vendor only to discover it costs more than expected.

quote.text: I like to see the prices of the food on the picture rather than clicking onto the restaurant page only to find out it's 30 euro.

pains.t: Ratings are hard for food delivery users to trust.
pains.w: A high star rating from a handful of reviewers reads as unreliable, and it's unclear why some vendors are surfaced as 'chosen'.

quote.text: I don't trust this one because even if it's 5 stars but only 1 review.

pains.t: Choice overload leaves indecisive food delivery users stuck.
pains.w: Facing too many options and not-always-relevant recommendations, indecisive users fall back on a familiar 'safe' restaurant — or abandon the order entirely.

pains.t: Deals are confusing — food delivery users can't tell what applies or how much they save.
pains.w: Overlapping incentives and unclear terms create overload; the discount bar is easy to miss and voucher comprehension is low, so users misjudge the real saving.

delights.t: Free-delivery filtering is a valued way for food delivery users to shop to budget.
delights.w: Every participant welcomed a free-delivery filter even when they didn't always need it — it maps to the budget lens they apply when deciding.

delights.t: A relevant deal both helps food delivery users decide and lifts the experience.
delights.w: Discounts help less-decisive users commit, and a good, applicable deal makes the order feel worth it.

quote.text: The discount is a plus point, but having the discounts is really uplifting.

delights.t: Reorder is a fast, trusted shortcut for food delivery users.
delights.w: Past orders and favourite restaurants take users straight to a known, safe choice with minimal effort.

quote.text: I just want my food and there's a way I order it and I want to order it that way every time.

delights.t: Reviews and photos give food delivery users the confidence to choose.
delights.w: Users lean heavily on ratings, written reviews and real dish photos to judge a new place before ordering.

quote.text: The first important thing for me is what people say about the restaurant.

jtbd.functional: Pay quickly and correctly, with the payment method I trust and the right voucher applied.
jtbd.emotional: Feel confident the price is final and fair — no surprises between cart and checkout.
jtbd.social: Get an order for the household over the line without hassle.

pains.t: Payment and checkout failures interrupt food delivery users.
pains.w: Checkout is harder for new users in SEQ analysis, and the top complaints are technical/app-performance errors and payment-method problems (~18%) — first-time failures that cost trust.

pains.t: Vouchers that looked available get rejected at the cart.
pains.w: Vouchers food delivery users expected are flagged expired, invalid or inapplicable at checkout, and amounts don't always match earlier screens.

pains.t: Prices change between cart and checkout, frustrating food delivery users.
pains.w: The vast majority (10/11) are frustrated by a difference between the cart total and the final checkout price.

pains.t: Applying the best voucher takes food delivery users too many manual steps.
pains.w: Users hunt for and apply the right voucher by hand; many (especially in TR) want it applied automatically.

pains.t: Reorder should be one tap, but it's buried for food delivery users.
pains.w: A top use case sits beneath promotions with no fast track from entry to checkout, so a one-tap job takes several.

pains.t: Food delivery users want more, more-reliable payment methods.
pains.w: Demand is clear for flexible options including postpaid / pay-later; onboarding tested as easy, but questions remain on credit and repayment.

delights.t: Google/Apple Pay is a fast, trusted checkout option for food delivery users.
delights.w: New users single it out as a welcome payment method — for some it's the reason they use the app over web.

delights.t: Cart-and-checkout is a relative strength for food delivery users.
delights.w: The split between reviewing the cart and finalising checkout matches users' mental model, and saved carts and pre-order confirmation are noticed and appreciated.

jtbd.functional: Know where my order is and a reliable time it will arrive.
jtbd.emotional: Feel reassured it's handled, and know I can get help fast if it isn't.
jtbd.social: Plan around the arrival so I'm ready when the food reaches me and others.

pains.t: Unreliable, jumping ETAs are the biggest CSAT gap to competitors.
pains.w: ~25% of orders run late (an estimated €25M GMV lost to cancellations), and inaccurate ETAs are the single largest driver of the CSAT gap versus rivals for food delivery users.

quote.text: I compare the ETA with Trendyol and leave Yemek... Yemeksepeti delivers in 45-60 mins, Trendyol in 15.

pains.t: Unclear order status is the #1 support-contact reason for food delivery users.
pains.w: Wrong or unclear status drives ~1.7M support contacts a year, with a 58% CSAT gap on restaurant orders.

pains.t: Pandora lags competitors on real-time rider location.
pains.w: Food delivery users rate Pandora below rivals on clear live updates (-12.4%) and knowing the rider's real-time location (-10%).

pains.t: Delays push food delivery users straight to a faster competitor.
pains.w: When the promised time slips with no clear reason, users switch to a rival offering the same restaurant faster.

jtbd.functional: Get my order, on time and in good condition — or a fast, fair resolution if not.
jtbd.emotional: Feel looked after at the door, and taken care of when something goes wrong.
jtbd.social: Have a good handover moment with the rider and share the meal I ordered.

pains.t: Food quality on arrival is a recurring letdown for food delivery users.
pains.w: Returning customers repeatedly cite food-quality issues on delivered orders as a frustration at the receiving moment.

pains.t: Cancellations are large-scale and poorly recovered for food delivery users.
pains.w: ~2.6% of orders are cancelled (~22M a year, ~€226M GMV lost); the screens do little to help users reorder or explore, and refund communication is weak.

pains.t: Support is the biggest experience gap to competitors for food delivery users.
pains.w: Support and issue resolution rate ~12% below rivals, and a poor support experience measurably reduces how often people order.

pains.t: Help forms can't capture the real problem for food delivery users.
pains.w: The help-center form misses case nuance (e.g. a missing item inside a set meal), pushing users to hunt for a live agent.

quote.text: There's no breakdown of the set, so I can't actually choose the item that's missing.

delights.t: The rider handover is a genuine emotional high point for food delivery users.
delights.w: The human moment at the door stands out, and most users actively want an after-delivery way to thank or tip the rider — reinforcing goodwill and reorder intent.

jtbd.functional: Restock what I need fast — heavy or urgent items — without a trip to the shop.
jtbd.emotional: Trust that groceries I can't physically inspect will still be fresh and good.
jtbd.social: Keep the household stocked with the brands and variety we rely on.

pains.t: Location and sign-up gate new QC users before they can explore.
pains.w: The shared onboarding asks for a location and pushes sign-up before showing value; evidence on location is mixed, but the block on exploring first is the common frustration.

pains.t: New QC users assume search is for restaurants, so the grocery path goes unused.
pains.w: New-to-QC users think search means restaurants and active users go straight to shop icons, so grocery discovery is bypassed.

pains.t: Many QC users believe one shop is all Pandora offers.
pains.w: A highlighted single-shop shortcut (e.g. d-mart) leads users to think it's the only grocery option, so they never explore the shop landing page and bounce when it lacks an item.

pains.t: Produce mistrust is a critical barrier for new QC users.
pains.w: Not being able to inspect freshness blocks trial (e.g. 49% TR, 40% SG, 26% HK), and produce trust is weak — new users rate it just 4.0/7.

quote.text: When I buy vegetables online, I can't see myself, but I want to know if the quality is good, fresh and not damaged.

pains.t: Affordability perception is the key barrier for new QC users.
pains.w: It blocks ~40% of new users and drives ~36% of existing users away — perceived high prices and fees, not lack of promos — so lower prices are the #1 acquisition trigger (62%).

quote.text: This is $50 and then you're telling me it was $75? I doubt it — the original price is a bit too much.

pains.t: Pandora is pigeonholed for urgent, small QC needs.
pains.w: Seen as a solution for small/urgent orders, so 37-45% of QC users switch to competitors or physical stores for larger, planned weekly hauls.

pains.t: Physical stores still out-pull the app on discovery for QC users.
pains.w: 32% find brick-and-mortar more inspiring to browse and 45% value the social side of shopping, drawing them away from the app.

pains.t: Pro and loyalty value is unclear to QC users.
pains.w: Pro's savings and loyalty rewards are hard to judge — many who'd break even never subscribe — and competitors' loyalty programs feel stronger.

pains.t: Supporting local shops is a barrier for some EU QC users.
pains.w: A preference for local, independent grocers holds users back from trying platform groceries in several EU markets.

delights.t: Reorder makes restock effortless for QC users.
delights.w: Previous orders are the natural starting point for recurring restock — users go straight from 'what's missing' to a familiar basket.

jtbd.functional: Get the specific items I need, fast and at the best price — ideally all in one basket.
jtbd.emotional: Feel I'm getting a good deal without turning it into a chore.
jtbd.social: Keep the household stocked with what everyone needs.

pains.t: Assortment is the #1 reason QC users churn to competitors.
pains.w: Gaps in variety, fresh produce and multi-vendor drive over 50% of existing users to rivals or back to physical stores, and out-of-stock items compound it.

pains.t: QC users can't find whole categories they want.
pains.w: Users leave because they can't find specialty foods (32%), household/cleaning (29%), personal care (17%) or baby products (15%).

pains.t: A shop-first layout forces QC users to do the price comparison themselves.
pains.w: 76% know the items they want before opening, but the shop-first structure makes them browse store by store and mentally aggregate prices.

quote.text: It's like for me it's another job to do... pick yogurt, and then whoever has the lower price then I choose.

pains.t: The anchor item dictates the shop, so QC users settle for a worse deal.
pains.w: Users pick the shop that stocks their most important item and accept the rest, rather than getting the best price across the basket.

quote.text: Otherwise I will just go with my familiar one... I will not be getting the best deal maybe.

pains.t: QC users can't judge product quality or value from the listing.
pains.w: Size, weight, expiry, per-unit price, images and nutrition are missing or unclear, forcing blind buys or a retreat to familiar items.

pains.t: Grocery deals are hard for QC users to find and understand.
pains.w: Offers like Mix & Match and Pro discounts are confusing, scattered and unclear in their terms, so users can't tell what applies while shopping.

pains.t: Peer reviews feel low-value to QC users, who want guarantees from Pandora.
pains.w: For everyday groceries, reading and writing peer reviews is high-effort/low-reward; users would rather Pandora guarantee freshness and safe delivery.

quote.text: It is nice to see feedback, but not nice to give it — I don't want to write long reviews.

pains.t: Counterfeit and authenticity fears deter QC users in Health & Beauty.
pains.w: Unreliable reviews and worries about fakes are real barriers in higher-stakes categories like Health & Beauty.

delights.t: Finding familiar or unique products is a bright spot for QC users.
delights.w: Locating trusted staples or special/unique items — including harder-to-find international brands — stands out in the selection experience.

delights.t: Discovering specialty shops surprises and delights QC users.
delights.w: Users are genuinely pleased to find pharmacy, deli, flowers and gift shops they didn't know Pandora offered.

delights.t: A valuable, relevant deal makes QC users feel they're shopping smart.
delights.w: Worthwhile discounts are a highlight of browsing groceries and reinforce the deal-driven reason many choose QC.

quote.text: Because I know there will be some products on discount, and it's going to be an advantage.

delights.t: Personalised search makes QC users feel understood.
delights.w: Surfacing 'Past Purchases' and favourites first, and cleanly separating shops from restaurants, delights users.

quote.text: I like it that someone already picked the best prices.

jtbd.functional: Check out fast and pay reliably, seeing my real savings before I commit.
jtbd.emotional: Feel in control of a larger basket without fear of a bad total or failed payment.
jtbd.social: Stock up for the whole household in one confident checkout.

pains.t: Payment failures are the primary technical barrier at QC checkout.
pains.w: Payment processing failures interrupt orders at the point of paying, highest in Turkey (16%).

pains.t: Fees and minimums punish QC users for ordering across shops.
pains.w: Delivery fee, MOV and Pro benefits make multi-shop baskets uneconomical (12/12 sessions), so users lock into one shop or delay.

pains.t: No multicart stops QC users shopping several stores at once.
pains.w: New-to-QC users don't understand why they can't add items from different shops to one cart — it breaks basic e-commerce expectations and leads to abandonment.

pains.t: QC users can't confirm their real savings in the cart.
pains.w: Understanding total savings and comparing value is hard, so users aren't sure what they're actually paying after discounts.

pains.t: Coupons are unclear or inconsistent for QC users.
pains.w: Discount amounts shown earlier don't always match the cart, and applying the right coupon takes manual effort.

delights.t: A clear cart-and-checkout flow keeps a big QC basket manageable.
delights.w: The cart/checkout separation matches how users think, and saved carts and multicart are noticed and appreciated.

jtbd.functional: Know when my groceries will arrive so I can plan around them.
jtbd.emotional: Feel reassured my order is on track without having to keep checking.
jtbd.social: Time the delivery for when the household needs the items.

pains.t: Late, unreliable delivery erodes QC users' trust.
pains.w: Delays and unreliable delivery times are a key waiting-stage frustration, with a ~28% CSAT gap for QC versus competitors.

pains.t: QC users are left without real-time updates.
pains.w: A lack of live updates and notifications means users keep re-opening the app to find out what's happening.

pains.t: Restock QC users want the delivery time known in advance.
pains.w: For planned restock, users want a dependable ETA up front so they can organise their day around it.

delights.t: A live map and progress updates reassure QC users while they wait.
delights.w: When present, map and progress indicators (and notifications, when enabled) reassure users and cut anxious re-checking.

jtbd.functional: Receive everything I ordered, fresh, correct and well packed.
jtbd.emotional: Trust the quality I couldn't inspect, and be recovered quickly if it's wrong.
jtbd.social: Keep the household supplied with items everyone can rely on.

pains.t: Poor-condition produce is a top receiving frustration for QC users.
pains.w: Damaged produce and item mismatches reinforce the very quality distrust that keeps people from ordering groceries online.

quote.text: I check the expiry date — it's always what I do when I go to physical shops.

pains.t: Careless packaging leaves QC users unsure everything arrived.
pains.w: Fresh, frozen and fragile items are packed together, plastic feels excessive, and there's no easy way to verify the full order was delivered.

pains.t: When a QC order goes wrong, cancellations and slow support let QC users down.
pains.w: Orders get cancelled for item unavailability, and when users need help, resolution lags competitors while forms can't capture the specific problem.

delights.t: Thoughtful packaging makes a QC order feel cared for.
delights.w: On-time delivery, considerate packaging and the occasional surprise in the bag make the receiving moment feel positive.

jtbd.functional: Save time and money by slotting a food run into my existing routine — commute, lunch break — without going out of my way.
jtbd.emotional: Stay in control of quality and skip the awkwardness of ordering in person or a failed delivery.
jtbd.social: Get in and out on my own terms, without crowds or awkward interaction.

pains.t: Delivery-only users see no compelling reason to try Pickup.
pains.w: Pro already makes delivery free and Pickup minimums aren't cheaper; survey data shows strong financial incentives are the #1 trigger for a first trial.

quote.text: It doesn't save that much time or money... at this moment there's no incentive for me.

pains.t: Real-world friction puts delivery-only users off Pickup.
pains.w: Traffic and parking make collecting feel like a hassle that isn't worth the effort.

quote.text: It's just ridiculous to lose time in the middle of traffic for the food.

pains.t: The way into Pickup is hidden, so new and light Pickup users miss it.
pains.w: The entry point sits in a secondary horizontal scroll and is easily missed, blocking a key path into Pickup (8/11).

quote.text: The pickup option was actually quite hard for me to find because I have to scroll... it's a little bit hidden.

pains.t: Low cross-vertical awareness caps Pickup's reach.
pains.w: Only ~60% in each market know Pandora offers non-food services at all, limiting how many even consider Pickup.

pains.t: Promo banners are dismissed as clutter by Pickup users.
pains.w: Banners are ignored as noise (assumed high minimum spend), so they fail to pull users into Pickup.

jtbd.functional: Quickly find a nearby, viable place and confirm the real, discounted price.
jtbd.emotional: Feel sure it's worth the trip before I commit to going.
jtbd.social: Pick something that works for whoever I'm collecting for.

pains.t: Pickup users apply strict logistical filters before price.
pains.w: Proximity, parking and rating are non-negotiable gates, but the app doesn't surface them, so users filter mentally and distrust the sorting.

quote.text: I will sort it by distance... those over 500m I won't consider actually.

pains.t: A broken, outdated map fails Pickup users.
pains.w: The map is low-value and out of date, so users can't rely on it to find nearby options.

quote.text: That map is really old... now it's only showing an empty place.

pains.t: Weak filters push Pickup users into tunnel vision.
pains.w: With filters feeling weak, users ignore most of the interface and only scan for discount tags or use Search — going blind to relevant options.

pains.t: Menu prices don't show the discounted Pickup price.
pains.w: Users can't trust the price reflects Pickup, so they treat high prices as a warning and add items to the cart just to check.

quote.text: Sometimes the price is not right because somehow it changed to delivery... so I just swap it to pickup.

pains.t: An unexpected switch back to Delivery breaks Pickup users' trust.
pains.w: The app sometimes reverts to Delivery mode, making users double-check everything and undermining confidence in the flow.

delights.t: Reorder and 'Popular' shortcuts let Pickup users choose fast.
delights.w: Heavy users lean on Reorder and lighter users on Popular/Recommendations to cut straight to a confident choice.

delights.t: Authentic food photos build Pickup users' trust in Pandora.
delights.w: Users easily spot competitors' AI-generated images and find them off-putting, raising trust in Pandora's more authentic imagery.

quote.text: 100% sure this is not going to be the meal.
quote.attribution: Pickup user, on a competitor's AI image

jtbd.functional: Lock in the best price and pay ahead so collection is instant.
jtbd.emotional: Feel confident I'm getting the best deal before I set off.
jtbd.social: Sort a quick solo grab on my own terms.

pains.t: Confirming the real discounted total is hard work for Pickup users.
pains.w: Discounts don't auto-apply and vouchers must be hunted manually, so users use the cart as a calculator to see the true price.

quote.text: Sometimes the app can't show the price after discount... so I put the food in my cart just to see the low price.

pains.t: Vouchers don't apply automatically for Pickup users.
pains.w: Users must manually find and apply the best voucher, adding effort right before they commit.

pains.t: Pickup users price-check rivals and abandon if Pandora is dearer.
pains.w: Value-seeking users build parallel carts in 2-3 competitor apps and churn at the last second if Pandora costs more, with low platform loyalty.

pains.t: Payment failures interrupt Pickup checkout.
pains.w: The shared checkout payment failures also hit Pickup orders at the point of payment.

delights.t: The app-suggested best voucher is a feature Pickup users trust.
delights.w: In the voucher step, the suggested best voucher is called out as a trusted, effort-saving help.

jtbd.functional: Know exactly when the order is ready and when to leave to collect it.
jtbd.emotional: Avoid wasting a trip or waiting around at the counter.
jtbd.social: Fit the pickup neatly into my routine and other commitments.

pains.t: Unreliable 'ready for collection' times are Pickup users' biggest frustration.
pains.w: The estimate is so inaccurate that users wait 10-30 minutes at the counter, erasing Pickup's time-saving promise; many now arrive late on purpose or call ahead.

quote.text: The app shows 10 minutes, but actually the waiting time is 20 minutes... I need to wait in front of the shop.

pains.t: No 'leave now' nudge leaves Pickup users guessing when to set off.
pains.w: Without a prompt tied to prep time, users estimate when to leave and often mistime the trip.

jtbd.functional: Find the counter and collect my correct order fast, without queueing.
jtbd.emotional: Feel the trip was worth it — quick, smooth and respectful of my time.
jtbd.social: Get in and out on my own terms, without crowds or awkward interaction.

pains.t: Scheduled Pickup orders arrive cold.
pains.w: When users schedule for later, restaurants often miss the pre-order flag and prepare hours early, so users collect cold food — breaking the core promise.

pains.t: Finding the in-store collection point is unclear for Pickup users.
pains.w: There's little in-app guidance on where to collect, so users are unsure where to go once they arrive.
